# Monte Carlo Simulation

Sensitivity analysis changes one input at a time. Scenario analysis changes a
few inputs together according to a story. Monte Carlo goes further by varying
every input according to probability distributions and running thousands of
simulations to produce a distribution of cash flows and an expected cash flow
for each year.

## Step 1: Specify the basic model

The first step is to identify the variables and relationships that describe the
model. The book gives an example model for Backyard Barbeques, Inc. (BBI) and
their brand new hydrogen grill. Cash flow is broken up into three parts:

### Annual revenue

$$
\begin{aligned}
\text{Number of grills sold}\\ \text{by entire industry}
\end{aligned}\ \ \times \ \
\begin{aligned}
\text{Market share of BBI's}\\ \text{hydrogen grill (in percent)}
\end{aligned}\ \ \times \ \
\begin{aligned}
\text{Price per}\\ \text{hydrogen grill}
\end{aligned}
$$

### Annual Cost

$$
\text{Fixed manufacturing costs}
\ \ + \ \
\text{Variable manufacturing costs}
\ \ + \ \
\text{Marketing costs}
\ \ + \ \
\text{Selling costs}
$$

### Initial investment

$$
\text{Cost of patent}
\ \ + \ \
\text{Test marketing costs}
\ \ + \ \
\text{Cost of production facility}
$$

## Step 2: Specify a distribution for each variable in the model

Using some research, you need to find reasonable values for the variables. This
should be done as a probability distribution. For example, the book identifies
the industry market size from a trade publication and gives a probability
distribution of three values. The values are 10, 11, and 12, with probabilities
20%, 60%, 20%.

The next variable is the market share of BBI. This is estimated with a long
right tail. Values: 1%, 2%, 3%, 4%, 5%, and 8% with probabilities 10%, 20%,
30%, 25%, 10%, and 5%.

The final variable defining the annual revenue is the price. If demand is high,
you can usually charge more. Therefore, price depends on the market size so we
must include that variable when defining price. The book describes a general
price of \$200. The price gets defined as:

$$
\begin{aligned}
\text{Next year's price}\\
\text{per hydrogen grill}
\end{aligned}
\begin{aligned}\ \ = \ \
\$190
\end{aligned}\ \ + \ \
\begin{aligned}
\$1
\end{aligned}\ \ \times \ \
\begin{aligned}
\text{Industry wide unit sales}\\
\text{(in millions)}
\end{aligned}\ \ + / - \ \
\$3
$$

With this definition of the price, we find the probability distributions (using
11 million as the market size as an example):

$$
\begin{aligned}
\$190 + \$11 + \$3 = \$204\ \ \text{(50\% probability)}\\
\$190 + \$11 - \$3 = \$198\ \ \text{(50\% probability)}
\end{aligned}
$$

With the variables of the first part defined, the next step is to define
the market size growth rate. The book defines three possible rates and their
probabilities: 1%, 3%, 5% with probabilities 20%, 60%, 20%.

The cost and initial investment parts of the model are not defined in the book,
but they would be defined in a similar manner.

Special attention will need to be paid to the interactions between the
variables because ineffective management will likely allow the different cost
components to rise together.

## Step 3: The Computer draws one outcome

The computer randomly draws one value from each distribution in Step 2. In the
book's example, the draws for next year are:

* Industry sales: 10 million grills
* BBI's market share: 2%
* Price shock: +\$3

Next year's price is then:

$$
\$190 + \$1 \times 10 + \$3 = \$203
$$

and next year's revenue is

$$
10 \text{ million} \times .02 \times \$203 = \$40.6 \text{ million}
$$

The computer draws the cost and investment variables the same way. For later
years it also draws a growth rate for industry sales. One complete draw gives
one possible cash-flow stream for the life of the project.

## Step 4: Repeat the procedure

Repeat Step 3 thousands of times generating more cash flow outcomes. The
results produce a distribution of cash flow for each future year. The
distribution is the basic output of the Monte Carlo simulation.

## Step 5: Calculate NPV

Discount each year's expected cash flow at the project's risk-adjusted rate
(its cost of capital), as in any NPV calculation.

## Conclusion

Monte Carlo simulations are powerful. This is because interactions between
variables are explicitly specified and by building the model the forecaster's
understanding is deepened. However, according to Graham and Harvey, only about
15 percent of firms use them for capital budgeting simulations. Executives are
frequently skeptical about their complexity. It is difficult to model either
the distributions of the variables or their relationships and the output is
often devoid of economic intuition. Therefore, it is not likely they will be
"the wave of the future."
